transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… what brings me in is I just can’t keep my mind on one thing anymore. It’s gotten really hard to do my work. Like, I’ll be fixing a rendering bug, and I’ll be right in the middle of a line of code, and then a Slack ping comes in—or honestly even just a color pattern on the screen catches my eye, or a siren goes by outside—and suddenly I’m pulled into some totally different idea before I’ve finished what I was doing.

It’s not like normal multitasking. I’m a software developer, so I’m used to having a lot going on, but this feels different. My attention just keeps getting yanked away, over and over, and then I realize I’ve left half-finished things everywhere. That’s the main reason I came in, because it’s starting to feel like I can’t trust my own focus.
When your focus gets pulled away like that, are you usually also feeling unusually energized or wound up?

Yeah. “Wound up” is actually a pretty good way to put it, although it doesn’t feel like just being anxious or something. It’s more like there’s this constant current running through me. I wake up and my brain is already moving—like before I’ve even really gotten out of bed, I’m planning code changes, thinking through feature ideas, then somehow I’m also picturing how something could be presented visually, like an exhibition layout, and then I’m thinking about how it would be talked about or framed publicly.

And sitting still feels… almost wrong. Like I’m wasting the moment if I’m not acting on one of those ideas right away. So when my focus gets pulled away, it’s not just that I’m distracted—it’s like there are five other things already lit up in my head, all feeling urgent or important. It makes it really hard to just stay with one task.
When this wound-up feeling happens, do you find that you need much less sleep than usual?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean… I know my sleep gets kind of pushed around when I’m wound up, because I’ll stay up later than I mean to, usually because my mind is still going and I keep thinking, “Okay, just one more thing,” or I’m trying to finish some thought before it slips away.

But in terms of whether I need much less sleep… I don’t know that I’ve tracked it carefully enough to say. It doesn’t always feel like I’m choosing not to sleep because I’m fine without it, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’m just not noticing the time, or I’m restless, or I lie there thinking through things. Then the next day I might still be running on that same energy for a while, but I’m not sure whether that means I needed less sleep or I was just kind of overriding being tired.

So… I’d say I’ve noticed sleep being affected, but I’m not sure I can confidently say how much less, or whether it’s every time.
During these wound-up periods, do you feel unusually confident or more capable than usual?

Yeah… yes, I do. And it’s not just like, “Oh, I’m having a good day” or “I wrote some clean code and feel proud of it.” It gets much bigger than that.

When I’m in that state, I start feeling like I can see connections other people just aren’t seeing. Like, I’ll be thinking about generative art, and then Mexican visual traditions—colors, patterns, public murals, the way images carry history—and then how the tech community is always talking about innovation but in this kind of sterile way. And I honestly start feeling like I’m the only one who can bring those worlds together in a way that actually matters.

Like… not just make a project, but change how the city thinks about public art. That sounds grandiose when I say it out loud, maybe, but in the moment it feels completely obvious. Like, of course I’m the person who can do it, because I can understand the coding side, the visual side, and the cultural side all at once. I’ll feel unusually capable, like I’m ahead of everyone else and they just haven’t caught up to the idea yet.
Do these wound-up, unusually confident periods come in clear episodes that feel different from your usual self?

Yeah, they do feel like episodes. I mean, I don’t know where the exact line is, but it’s not just my normal personality turned up a little. Most days when I’m in it, I feel… lit up, like there’s this sense that everything is finally aligning. Like Glendale is finally catching up with what I’ve been building in my head, and I’m just supposed to move fast enough to meet it.

And it feels different from my usual self because usually I can step back, I can listen, I can tolerate people wanting meetings or planning or whatever. But during those stretches, if my wife or coworkers slow me down with what they call “process,” I snap really hard. Like I get instantly irritated because it feels like they’re putting cones in front of a fire truck, you know? I’m thinking, “Why are we debating this? The thing is right there. We should already be doing it.”

So yes, it comes as this state where I’m unusually charged and confident, but also way more easily frustrated when anyone gets in the way. It’s not how I am all the time.
During those lit-up periods, do you feel rested after only a few hours of sleep?

I’m not totally sure. That’s the part that’s hard for me to pin down, because I don’t know if I’d say I feel rested exactly.

There are nights during those periods where I’ll only sleep a little, or I’ll get to bed really late and wake up earlier than I expected, and for a while I can sort of pop up and keep going. Like my brain starts running before I’ve even had time to notice whether I’m tired. But if you’re asking, “Do I wake up after three or four hours and feel genuinely refreshed, like I had a full night’s sleep?” I don’t know that I can say that confidently.

It’s more like the momentum carries me. I may not feel sleepy in the normal way, or I ignore it because there’s something I want to think about or do. But I’m not sure that’s the same as feeling rested. I haven’t really tracked it carefully, so I don’t want to give you a cleaner answer than I actually have.
During those lit-up periods, do you find yourself talking much more than usual?

Yeah, definitely. That one is pretty noticeable, actually, because people have pointed it out to me.

When I start explaining the platform or the project, I don’t just say the simple version. I’ll start with, like, the architecture—how the system should be structured, what data it needs, how the generative part would work—and then before anyone can respond I’m already talking about funding, and then the public art angle, and then how it could be deployed across Glendale, and then the cultural impact, and who should be involved, and why the timing matters.

And in my head it all feels connected, so it doesn’t feel like I’m rambling. It feels like I’m finally saying the whole thing properly. But other people will be like, “Can I jump in?” or my wife will say, “You haven’t let me finish a sentence.” Coworkers have told me they can’t really get a word in when I’m like that.

To me it feels like the thoughts are arriving too fast to pause. Like if I stop, I’ll lose the thread, or the energy of it will drop, so I just keep going. And I know that probably sounds exhausting from the outside, but in the moment it feels urgent, like I have to get the entire map out while I can still see it.
During these lit-up periods, has your behavior ever caused serious problems at work, at home, or with the law?

Yeah. I mean, I wish I could say it was just people overreacting to me being intense, but… no, it’s caused real problems.

At work, the biggest one was that I bypassed the normal approval process and pushed changes myself. In my head at the time, it felt completely justified, like waiting for review was going to kill the momentum and everyone else was being too slow or too cautious. I remember thinking, “This is obviously the right move, and once they see it working, they’ll understand.” But that is not how it landed. My employer ended up putting me on leave because of it. And I can say now that I understand why that was a big deal, but at the time I really felt like I was solving a problem, not creating one.

And at home it’s been bad too. My wife has told me the spending and the arguments make things feel unstable, like she doesn’t know what version of me she’s going to get or whether I’m going to make some big decision without really talking it through. I tend to see it as investing in the idea or moving things forward, but for her it feels reckless, and then when she questions it I get defensive and it turns into a fight.

No legal trouble, at least not that I can think of. But work and home, yes. It’s definitely crossed the line from “I’m just excited” into consequences.
During those lit-up periods, have you ever had experiences like hearing or seeing things other people didn’t, or beliefs that others said were unrealistic or not true?

Yeah… not so much hearing voices or seeing things, at least not like that. But the beliefs part, yes. And it’s hard to talk about because even saying it out loud, part of me knows how it sounds.

During those periods, I get very convinced that certain people or organizations are aware of what I’m building and are kind of… circling it quietly. Like major museums, a couple of investors, people who have influence in that space. It doesn’t feel like a vague hope, it feels like I’m noticing a pattern that other people are missing.

For example, I’ll see language in a museum showcase or on an Instagram post and it lines up almost too perfectly with the language I’ve been using about the platform. Or I’ll get an email at work where the timing or phrasing seems connected, like it’s indirectly referencing what I’m doing without saying it outright. And when several of those things happen close together, I’ll feel sure it can’t just be coincidence.

My wife will say, “That’s a stretch,” or “They’re not talking to you,” or “You’re connecting things that aren’t connected.” But in the moment I don’t experience it as a stretch. I experience it like I’m the only one paying close enough attention. Like there’s this quiet interest building around the project, and people are signaling around it because they don’t want to come out directly yet.

So, no, I don’t think I’ve had, like, hallucinations. But beliefs that other people tell me are unrealistic or not true? Yeah. That has happened.
